newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austrian conservatives vote for NATO entry.
newsitem.headline: Austrian conservatives vote for NATO entry.

text.p: The conservative half of Austria's ruling coalition came out on Monday in favour of joining NATO, widening a rift within the government about how to adapt neutral Austria's security policy as the alliance expands.

"Austria ought to become a part of 'new' NATO -- the community of our partners dedicated to political peace and stability," the People's Party said in a policy document approved unanimously at a leadership meeting.

NATO's decision at its summit in Madrid last week to invite the Czech Republic and Hungary -- two of Austria's formerly communist neighbours -- and Poland to join the alliance, probably in 1999, had added to the pressure on neutral Austria to rethink its position.
"We want to seize the opportunity -- before 1999," said Wolfgang Schuessel, People's Party leader and foreign minister.

But the senior coalition partner, Prime Minister Viktor Klima's Social Democrats, are highly sceptical and insist a referendum should precede any decision is taken to scrap Austria's cherished neutrality, enshrined in the constitution. Opinion polls show a comfortable majority of Austrians oppose the idea.
"I don't see any difference between the 'new' NATO and the old military alliance," Transport Minister Caspar Einem, a senior member of the Social Democrats, told state radio.
The government is due to present recommendations on the NATO issue next year.
The People's Party, which opposes holding a referendum, has been arguing increasingly emphatically that national security can best be served by membership of an international alliance.
"It is more efficient and cost effective...and would be of benefit to the economy," the policy document said.
Over the weekend President Thomas Klestil, a member of the People's Party, said that "staying out of the security community could have fatal consequences for us in the future".
And conservative Defence Minister Werner Fasslabend said the government must agree on a common position as soon as possible to let it take part in NATO's expansion process.

The People's Party policy document also backed membership of the European Union's defence arm, the Western European Union, but opposed the stationing of foreign troops or nuclear weapons on Austrian soil.
